entries.subject: ALMA science archive: ObsCore TAP, DataLink and file downloads
entries.finding: Public ALMA data can be queried and downloaded anonymously. DataLink lists each member OUS's product tarball and the files inside it, each downloadable on its own: R Dor's 2023 band-7 continuum image (2022.1.01071.S, uid://A001/X35f5/Xaea) is a 33 MB FITS file inside a 77 GB product tarball, beside 464 GB of raw ASDM.

entries.subject: ALMA proprietary period and anonymous access
entries.finding: ALMA data are proprietary for 12 months, after which access and download are anonymous.

entries.subject: CASA and the ALMA imaging pipeline
entries.finding: CASA processes ALMA data and is distributed by NRAO under GPL v3 or later; its size and macOS support were not checked. Re-imaging from raw data does not fit on this machine (R Dor band 7 alone is 464 GB of raw measurement sets), so the first route is the archive's own continuum images, which the pipeline already produced.
entries.revisitWhen: The archive continuum images are inspected and show surface structure worth re-imaging, or a calibrated measurement set becomes downloadable on its own.

entries.subject: Public long-baseline ALMA data on resolved giant stars
entries.finding: ObsCore lists public data at 30 mas resolution or finer on Betelgeuse (9.7 mas, 2022.A.00026.S, July 2023), R Dor (14.9 mas, 2022.1.01071.S, July and August 2023, the months Vlemmings et al. 2024 report; the paper's data statement not checked) and Mira (14.5 mas, 2022.1.00817.S and 2022.1.01071.S). Nothing downloaded yet; the archive images stack several dates and are not self-calibrated, and a spotless check for images rather than visibilities does not exist.
entries.revisitWhen: The archive continuum images of R Dor, Betelgeuse and Mira are downloaded and inspected.

entries.subject: What this archive holds for catalogued bodies
entries.finding: The same screen matched 26 bodies in the ALMA archive, 17,934 rows, mostly bands 3, 6 and 7. The screen ranked Pallas and Juno as the strongest unphotographed candidates at roughly 20 and 10 beams across; checked against the observations that exist, on 17 September 2026, both numbers are wrong. The screen divided each body's size at its closest possible approach by the instrument's finest resolution, and neither body was ever observed under those conditions. The finest resolution ALMA actually used is 60.6 milliarcseconds on Pallas over 1,323 rows and 174.2 on Juno over 24, which puts Pallas at about 4.5 beams across its disc at the epochs observed and Juno at 0.8: Juno is never resolved at all. Pallas is a flux calibrator in 1,295 of its rows, and the pipeline images bandpass, phase and check-source calibrators only, so no image of it exists to take. Its finest execution is a 19-antenna single 151-second scan with no auxiliary products; the best one that could be reduced is 3.6 beams. Polaris was turned down at about six.
entries.revisitWhen: Pallas, Juno or another ALMA candidate is taken up.
